title: Trump Media Sells Fast Access to Truth Social Posts Through Truth API
description_medium: Trump Media launched Truth API on August 1, 2026, offering businesses a real-time feed of Truth Social posts, including market-sensitive presidential announcements. The New Yorker reported that more than ten customers, mostly high-frequency trading firms, had signed up by mid-August, with pricing reportedly reaching $100,000 per month. Media groups later sued, arguing the service gave paying clients preferential access to presidential statements. Ethics critics warned of conflicts; Trump Media said it was not doing anything wrong.
description_long: A New Yorker column published August 17, 2026, examined Truth API, a Trump Media & Technology Group product that sells fast access to posts on President Donald Trump’s Truth Social account. The company described it as a licensed, real-time feed of posts that could move markets, such as announcements on tariffs, the Federal Reserve, or Middle East policy. Trump is the company’s largest shareholder, though the White House said he does not manage his businesses and the company said the product was lawful. The service launched August 1, and Trump Media’s interim chief executive told investors that more than ten customers had signed up, most of them high-frequency trading firms. The New Yorker reported that subscriptions could cost up to $100,000 monthly. Senator Mark Warner urged financial trade associations not to legitimize the service, and two media organizations, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, filed a federal lawsuit arguing that Truth API denied journalists equal access to presidential statements. Ethics specialists quoted in the column said preferential access could create conflicts of interest or insider-trading concerns, while the company compared its product to other social-media data feeds. The dispute centers on a president’s social-media business selling earlier access to communications that can affect markets. The article reported allegations and legal questions; it did not establish a court finding that the service violated securities or ethics laws.

corrected_wording.original_claim: Trump amassed $2.2 billion in income during his second term as president.
corrected_wording.corrected: The cited Guardian report says estimates put Trump’s 2025 business revenue at $2.2 billion; revenue is not equivalent to personal income or profit. The New Yorker article linked in this record specifically concerns Truth API and its sale of early access to posts.

source_access_notes: Opened the supplied New Yorker column and Guardian report. The record conflated the column’s Truth API subject with a separate estimate of 2025 business revenue; the descriptions focus on the linked event and clarify the figure in corrected_wording.
rationale: Used the linked New Yorker article as the event and separated its Truth API reporting from a broader $2.2 billion revenue figure misdescribed as presidential income.

title: Trump Signs Revised Travel Ban Executive Order 13780
description_medium: On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing the initial January travel-ban order after that order was blocked in court. The revised order temporarily suspended entry for some nationals of six countries—Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen—and paused refugee admissions for 120 days, with exceptions and case-by-case waivers. Iraq was removed from the list. The order was scheduled to take effect March 16, but a federal court blocked it before implementation.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017, revising the travel and refugee restrictions in his January 27 order after federal courts halted key parts of the first version. The new directive called for a 90-day suspension of entry for certain nationals from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen while the government reviewed screening procedures. It removed Iraq from the list and included exceptions for lawful permanent residents, people with specified valid visas or travel documents, dual nationals traveling on a non-designated passport, and others. The order also suspended the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for 120 days, while permitting case-by-case waivers. It directed agencies to review foreign governments’ information-sharing practices and recommend additional restrictions or removals. The administration presented the policy as a national-security measure; opponents challenged it as discriminatory and unlawful. The order was set to take effect on March 16, 2017, but a federal judge in Hawaii issued a nationwide temporary restraining order the day before, blocking its central provisions. The order therefore became the revised form of Trump’s travel ban, but its initial entry restrictions did not take effect on schedule. Later litigation over the administration’s authority and purpose continued beyond the signing event.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The linked White House source documents the revised Executive Order 13780 signed March 6, 2017.
corrected_wording.corrected: The supplied link is for the January 27 original order, Executive Order 13769. The March 6 revised order is Executive Order 13780; it covered six countries after removing Iraq and did not take effect as scheduled because a court blocked it.

source_access_notes: The supplied White House URL is the January 27 EO 13769, not the revised EO 13780. Used the official March 6 text hosted by GovInfo and DHS’s contemporaneous FAQ for the corrected order and timing.
rationale: Replaced the mismatched primary-source link as the basis for the text by consulting the correct March 6 order and distinguishing its signed date from its blocked effective date.

title: Ethics Critics Raise Emoluments Concerns Over Trump’s Business Interests
description_medium: Legal and ethics experts have questioned whether benefits connected to Donald Trump’s businesses create conflicts with the Constitution’s foreign-emoluments restriction. Reported examples include a $400 million aircraft gifted by Qatar, foreign investment in Trump-linked companies, and cryptocurrency ventures. Trump’s critics argue that such benefits require scrutiny, but the reports do not establish that every business payment violates the clause or cite a court ruling resolving the allegations.
description_long: A 2026 report on presidential business interests described concern among legal and ethics experts about Donald Trump’s continued ties to businesses while in office. The Guardian cited cryptocurrency investments, foreign-linked hotel and golf ventures, and a $400 million aircraft provided by Qatar as examples critics said raised conflicts of interest and questions under the Constitution’s Foreign Emoluments Clause. That clause restricts federal officeholders from accepting certain benefits from foreign states without congressional consent; whether a particular transaction falls within the rule depends on its structure, recipient, and legal treatment. The report also described Trump Media’s plan to sell financial firms faster access to Truth Social posts, a separate domestic business arrangement that critics said could profit from presidential communications. The cited experts argued that Trump’s business holdings, foreign relationships, and presidential decision-making created opportunities for self-dealing. Trump and administration representatives have denied wrongdoing and said applicable conflict-of-interest rules are being followed. The reporting uses critics’ accounts to frame a broader ethics dispute; it does not establish that each listed benefit was an unlawful emolument, nor does it identify a final court decision finding Trump liable under the clause. The record’s description should therefore present the examples as ethics concerns and constitutional allegations, rather than settled violations.

corrected_wording.original_claim: Trump’s crypto, airplane, and other ventures violated the Emoluments Clause, which prohibits federal officials from receiving gifts or payments from foreign governments.
corrected_wording.corrected: Critics argue that certain foreign-linked benefits connected to Trump’s businesses may raise Foreign Emoluments Clause concerns. The cited reporting does not establish that each payment or venture is covered or that a court found a violation.

source_access_notes: The supplied Slate URL could not be opened. The Guardian’s same-event reporting was accessible and supports the examples and attribution to ethics critics; it does not establish a legal violation.
rationale: Reframed the categorical constitutional-violation claim as an attributed ethics concern and clarified that the foreign-emoluments question is transaction-specific.

title: Supreme Court Denies Trump Rehearing Request in E. Jean Carroll Case
description_medium: On August 17, 2026, the Supreme Court denied Donald Trump’s request to rehear its refusal to review the $5 million civil verdict for E. Jean Carroll. A New York jury had found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming Carroll; with accrued interest, she received about $5.62 million in July. The denial ended his challenge to that verdict. A separate $83.3 million defamation judgment remained on appeal.
description_long: The Supreme Court on August 17, 2026, rejected Donald Trump’s request to reconsider its June decision not to hear his appeal of a $5 million civil verdict won by writer E. Jean Carroll. The jury verdict followed a 2023 trial in which jurors found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll in a Manhattan department-store dressing room in the 1990s and defaming her after she publicly described the assault. The jury applied the civil standard of proof; Trump denied the allegations. His lawyers argued that statements he made about Carroll while president were protected by presidential immunity, but the Supreme Court’s denial left the verdict in place without issuing a new explanation of the underlying facts. Carroll received roughly $5.62 million, including interest, after a federal judge ordered the escrowed funds released in July. Trump had separately tried to delay or recover the money as he continued his appeals, but the payment had already been distributed before the rehearing request was denied. The Supreme Court action concerns this $5 million case, not a separate jury award of $83.3 million in another Carroll defamation suit. That larger judgment remained the subject of a different appeal. The ruling closed Trump’s route to Supreme Court review of the first verdict, while litigation over the separate award continued.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The Supreme Court denied Trump’s attempt to claw back $5.6 million from Carroll.
corrected_wording.corrected: On August 17 the Court denied Trump’s rehearing request concerning the $5 million verdict. Carroll had already received about $5.62 million including interest; a separate $83.3 million judgment was still being appealed.

source_access_notes: The supplied Daily Mail page was blocked by robots.txt. Used the Supreme Court docket, CBS reporting, and a later Guardian update on the same case and payment history.
rationale: Corrected the headline’s “claw back” description by distinguishing the Court’s denial of rehearing from the earlier payment disbursement and separating the $83.3 million case.

title: Trump Cites Military and Security Features to Defend White House Ballroom Project
description_medium: As courts questioned whether Trump could build a ballroom without Congress, the administration increasingly described the East Wing project as an integrated military and security complex. Court filings cited a subterranean facility, hardened materials, a drone port, and sniper positions, while Trump posted renderings and called the site a military asset. These features were presented as national-security justifications in a legal dispute; the reporting distinguishes government claims and designs from established construction facts.
description_long: In August 2026, the Trump administration expanded its public and legal defense of the White House East Wing construction project by emphasizing military and security functions beneath and around the planned ballroom. The Independent reported that Trump described the project as a “Military Complex/Ballroom” and shared renderings for a rooftop drone port. Department of Justice filings cited an underground bunker, protected ventilation, blast-resistant materials, a drone facility, and sniper positions as parts of an integrated security project. The administration argued those features were needed to protect the president, officials, and visitors, including against potential attacks. Those claims came as federal courts had ordered the government to stop portions of above-ground ballroom construction unless Congress authorized the work; the administration appealed and argued the project had already received sufficient authority. The administration’s description reframed a privately promoted event space as a national-security facility, while opponents and preservation groups challenged the unilateral demolition of the historic East Wing and the claim that the ballroom itself was necessary. The legal question concerned presidential authority and construction on federal property as well as the asserted security needs. The filings and public renderings document what officials said and proposed, but the article does not independently verify every claimed defensive feature or show that the entire military complex was complete. In the following days, the Supreme Court allowed construction to proceed while the broader challenge continued.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The stalled ballroom project was a military complex, as administration officials established through court filings.
corrected_wording.corrected: Trump and administration lawyers described the planned ballroom site as an integrated military and security complex; their filings cited proposed features while courts were still considering the project’s authorization.

source_access_notes: Opened The Independent report. Added its later same-event Supreme Court update to avoid leaving the construction status frozen at the pre-ruling appeal stage.
rationale: Summarized the change in the administration’s national-security framing, attributed technical claims to court filings and distinguished design and argument from verified completion.
